Description: A black stone seal announced in 2024, found in Israel Antiquities Authority and City of David excavations along the southern wall of the Temple Mount, in First Temple-period debris. Its centre is a finely carved winged figure in Assyrian style, a protective 'genie' of the kind known from Neo-Assyrian art of the 9th-7th centuries BC and the first such figure found in Israeli and regional archaeology, framed by a paleo-Hebrew inscription reading 'Belonging to Yehoezer, son of Hoshayahu'. A hole drilled through its length let it be worn on a chain, so it served both as a personal seal and as an amulet. Researchers believe the seal began as the amulet of Hoshayahu, a senior official of the kingdom of Judah, and that his son Yeho'ezer inherited it and added both names. The seal is dated to about 700 BC.
Interpretations: The seal is a window into Judah as an Assyrian vassal: a Judahite administrator wore an Assyrian protective figure, made by a local craftsman at a high artistic level, as his mark of authority. Its names are parallels, not identifications: Yeho'ezer resembles Yo'ezer, one of David's warriors (1 Chronicles 12:7), and Hoshayahu resembles Azariah ben Hoshaiah of Jeremiah 43:2, but neither match is the seal's owner, and the entry claims no biblical identification for either man.
BiblicalSignificance: The seal shows the Yahwistic naming, the administration and the Assyrian artistic influence of Judah's elite in the century of Isaiah and Hezekiah, without claiming a biblical identity it cannot support.
DiscoveryLocation: Southern wall of the Temple Mount, Jerusalem, Israel
